questions.q: Why is a Kubernetes Secret's base64-encoded data not actually a security control?
options: Base64 is a form of strong encryption
Base64 is only an encoding, trivially decodable by anyone who can read the Secret object, not encryption
Kubernetes Secrets cannot be read by anyone, ever
Base64 encoding is deprecated and no longer used
questions.explain: Base64 just represents binary-safe data in YAML; it is decodable in one command, so real protection depends on RBAC and, ideally, encryption at rest in etcd.

questions.q: What does the External Secrets Operator pattern accomplish?
options: It deletes Kubernetes Secrets automatically after one use
It syncs a Kubernetes Secret automatically from a real vault, keeping the vault as the source of truth instead of manual copying
It replaces the need for any vault entirely
It encrypts all pod network traffic
questions.explain: A controller watches an ExternalSecret resource and keeps a Kubernetes Secret synced from the real vault automatically, removing the manual copy-and-forget-to-update step.

questions.q: In GitHub Actions, how is a secret typically referenced in a workflow file?
options: By writing its literal value directly into the YAML
Through the secrets context, such as ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}, without the value ever appearing in the workflow file
By storing it in a public environment variable file
Secrets cannot be used in GitHub Actions workflows
questions.explain: Secrets are referenced through the secrets context, and GitHub Actions automatically masks matching values in log output — though this masking is a safety net, not a guarantee.

questions.q: Why is GitHub Actions' automatic log masking described as "a safety net, not a guarantee"?
options: Because masking never works at all
Because it matches the literal secret value, so a transformed version (like a base64-encoded copy) can still slip past the mask
Because masking only applies to secrets longer than 50 characters
Because masking is disabled by default in all workflows
questions.explain: The masking matches the literal known secret value; if a script transforms the value before printing it, the transformed output may not be caught, so scripts should never deliberately print secrets regardless of masking.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what actually protects a secret sitting in an environment variable inside a running pod?
options: Environment variables are inherently unreadable by any process
The full chain end to end — vault access control, RBAC on who can read the Secret object, and care about what the application logs
Nothing; environment variables should never be used for secrets
Kubernetes automatically encrypts all environment variables
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes considering the whole chain — vault access control, Lesson 8's RBAC on the Secret object, and application-level logging discipline — rather than any single control being sufficient on its own.
